punnett.title: Punnett Square
punnett.description: A Punnett square lists possible allele combinations from two parents at one gene locus. This model assumes equal gamete probabilities, random fertilisation and complete dominance. Ratios describe expected probabilities across many offspring, not a guaranteed set of four children.
punnett.alleleHint: Use a capital letter for the dominant allele (e.g., B) and lowercase for recessive (b). Try BB × bb, Bb × Bb, AA × aa, etc.
punnett.invalidHint: Use two alleles of the same locus in both parents, for example Bb × bb; do not mix A and B.

contrast.en: Genotype is genetic constitution; phenotype is an observable characteristic influenced by genotype and environment.

cellDiagram.title: Animal and plant cell diagram
cellDiagram.description: Compare a typical animal cell with a photosynthetic plant cell. The diagram is simplified: it omits many components, and specialised cells can look different.
cellDiagram.plantExtras: The photosynthetic plant cell in this diagram has three extra parts: a cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts and a large central vacuole.
cellDiagram.hoverHint: Tap or hover a part to see its function.

nucleus.label: Nucleus
nucleus.desc: Holds the cell's DNA. Pores in the nuclear envelope let molecules, such as mRNA, pass in and out.

nucleolus.label: Nucleolus
nucleolus.desc: Nuclear region where ribosomal RNA is made and ribosomal subunits are assembled.

mitochondria.label: Mitochondria
mitochondria.desc: Most stages of aerobic respiration take place here. The energy released is stored in ATP.

ribosome.label: Ribosomes
ribosome.desc: Makes proteins by joining amino acids in the order set by mRNA. It has no membrane around it.

membrane.label: Cell membrane
membrane.desc: Controls which substances enter and leave the cell. It is a phospholipid bilayer with proteins in it.

cytoplasm.label: Cytoplasm
cytoplasm.desc: Water-based fluid between the cell membrane and the nucleus. Organelles are suspended in it, and many chemical reactions happen here.

wall.label: Cell wall
wall.desc: Rigid layer outside the cell membrane. It stops the cell from bursting when water enters.

chloroplast.label: Chloroplast
chloroplast.desc: Site of photosynthesis. Chlorophyll in the thylakoid membranes absorbs light.

vacuole.label: Vacuole
vacuole.desc: Large sac filled with cell sap. It stores water and dissolved substances and keeps the cell firm.

contrast.en: The cell wall lies outside the cell membrane and does not replace it. Plant cells have both.
contrast.ru: Клеточная стенка лежит снаружи клеточной мембраны и не заменяет её. У растительных клеток есть и стенка, и мембрана.

heartDiagram.title: Heart Diagram
heartDiagram.description: Trace pulmonary and systemic circulation through the four heart chambers. Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins return it. The colour indicates relative oxygen content, not the blood's actual colour.
heartDiagram.hoverHint: Hover a chamber or vessel to see its function.
heartDiagram.doubleCirc: Double circulation: blood passes the heart TWICE per circuit — once for the body, once for the lungs.

ra.label: Right atrium
ra.desc: Receives deoxygenated blood from the body via the vena cava.

rv.label: Right ventricle
rv.desc: Pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs via the pulmonary artery.

la.label: Left atrium
la.desc: Receives oxygenated blood from the lungs via pulmonary veins.

lv.label: Left ventricle
lv.desc: Pumps oxygenated blood to the entire body via the aorta. Thickest wall (high pressure).

vc.label: Vena cava
vc.desc: The superior and inferior venae cavae return relatively oxygen-poor blood from the body to the right atrium.

pa.label: Pulmonary artery
pa.desc: Carries relatively oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle to the lungs; arteries are defined by flow away from the heart.

pv.label: Pulmonary vein
pv.desc: Carries relatively oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the left atrium; veins return blood to the heart.

ao.label: Aorta
ao.desc: Largest artery. Carries oxygenated blood from left ventricle → body.

contrast.en: Arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins towards it; these names do not specify oxygen content.
contrast.ru: Артерии несут кровь от сердца, вены — к нему; названия не определяются содержанием кислорода.

photoDepth.title: Photosynthesis — deeper
photoDepth.body: In chloroplasts, light-dependent reactions in thylakoid membranes use light energy to make ATP and NADPH and release oxygen from water. The Calvin cycle in the stroma uses ATP and NADPH to fix CO₂ into small carbohydrates from which sugars can be made. It does not require darkness.

contrast.en: Carbon dioxide and water supply matter; light supplies energy. Plants also respire in both light and darkness.
contrast.ru: Углекислый газ и вода поставляют вещество, свет — энергию. Растения дышат и на свету, и в темноте.

hormones.title: Hormones in depth
items: Insulin from pancreatic beta cells promotes glucose uptake in responsive tissues and storage, lowering blood glucose.
Glucagon from pancreatic alpha cells promotes liver glucose production and release.
Adrenaline helps coordinate acute responses such as increased heart activity and fuel mobilisation.
Oestrogens and testosterone influence reproductive development and other functions in all sexes.
Thyroid hormones affect metabolic activity in many tissues.

contrast.en: A hormone is a signalling molecule; its target cells respond because they have suitable receptors.
contrast.ru: Гормон — сигнальная молекула; клетки-мишени отвечают на него благодаря соответствующим рецепторам.

genetics.title: Genetics — mutations and codons
genetics.body: An mRNA codon is a three-nucleotide sequence specifying an amino acid or a stop signal. AUG usually initiates translation and specifies methionine. Mutations change DNA: insertions or deletions shift a coding reading frame only when their length is not a multiple of three.

biotech.title: Biotechnology
items: Selective breeding chooses parents to change inherited traits over generations.
Genetic engineering directly alters DNA; it includes editing within one species and transfer between species.
Cloning produces genetically matching copies; mutations and environment can still create differences.
CRISPR-based editing targets selected sequences but requires checks for unintended changes.
Ethical assessment considers evidence, consent, welfare, environmental effects and access.

contrast.en: Biotechnology is broader than genetic engineering; engineering can edit existing DNA without adding a gene from another species.
contrast.ru: Биотехнология шире генной инженерии; инженерное изменение ДНК не обязательно переносит ген другого вида.

homeostasis.title: Homeostasis
homeostasis.body: Homeostasis is regulation of internal conditions within ranges compatible with cell function despite disturbances. Negative feedback reduces a deviation: a sensor detects change, a control system coordinates a response and effectors act. Conditions fluctuate around regulated values rather than staying perfectly constant.

cells.title: Cell Biology
cells.intro: All living organisms are made of cells, the basic unit of life. Animal and plant cells share many structures but differ from each other, and specialised cells are adapted to their functions.

light.name: Light microscope
light.rule: A light microscope forms a magnified image using visible light and lenses. Magnification is image size ÷ actual size. Resolution is the smallest distance between two points at which they can still be seen as separate. A conventional light microscope has a resolution of about 0.2 μm. If two points are not resolved, enlarging the image adds no detail.
examples: Eyepiece ×10 multiplied by objective ×40 gives total magnification ×400.
With a light microscope you can see whole plant and animal cells, nuclei, chloroplasts and vacuoles. In a living sample you can also see the cytoplasm moving.
A conventional light microscope cannot resolve ribosomes, mitochondrial internal detail or the thickness of the lipid bilayer.
Two points 0.1 μm apart merge into one blurred spot in a light microscope, because its resolution is about 0.2 μm.
light.tip: The smaller the resolution limit, the finer the detail you can see. A microscope with a limit of 0.2 μm shows more detail than one with a limit of 1 μm.

contrast.en: Magnification is a ratio with no unit, such as ×400. Resolution is a distance, such as 0.2 μm.
contrast.ru: Увеличение — безразмерная величина, например ×400. Предел разрешения — расстояние, например 0,2 мкм.

electron.name: Electron microscope
electron.rule: An electron microscope forms an image using a beam of electrons and electromagnetic lenses. Its resolving power is much higher than that of a light microscope. A transmission electron microscope (TEM) shows the internal structure of thin specimens, while a scanning electron microscope (SEM) shows surface detail. Conventional preparation and the vacuum inside the microscope prevent observation of living cells.
examples: A TEM image of a thin section shows the internal membranes of a mitochondrion.
A SEM image shows the surface shape of a pollen grain.
electron.watchOut: Resolution depends on instrument and specimen preparation; there is no single maximum magnification for all electron microscopes.

contrast.en: Electron micrographs are black and white. Colour is added later and does not show the true colour of the specimen.
contrast.ru: Электронные микрофотографии чёрно-белые. Цвет на них добавляют позже, и он не показывает настоящий цвет образца.

preparation.name: Preparing a wet mount
preparation.rule: A wet mount holds a thin specimen in liquid between a slide and coverslip. Lower the coverslip at an angle to reduce bubbles, then locate and focus the specimen with the lowest-magnification objective. A suitable stain increases contrast but may kill cells or alter structures.
examples: A thin layer of onion epidermis is placed in a drop of water and covered with a coverslip.
Iodine solution is a common stain for onion cells. It colours the nucleus, so the nucleus is easier to see.
preparation.tip: Lower the objective slowly while watching from the side, so that the lens does not hit the coverslip.

contrast.en: A wet mount is only for light microscopes. Electron microscope samples are fixed and placed in a vacuum, and TEM samples are also cut into ultrathin sections.
contrast.ru: Временный препарат годится только для светового микроскопа. Образцы для электронного микроскопа фиксируют и помещают в вакуум, а образцы для TEM, кроме того, режут на ультратонкие срезы.

drawing.name: Biological drawings
drawing.rule: A biological drawing shows only the structures that you actually observed, with clear outlines, labels and a title. Include a scale bar or the magnification of the drawing. When you calculate magnification, use image size and actual size in the same units. If the drawing is resized, its magnification changes, so the microscope setting no longer applies to it.
examples: A drawing of one onion epidermal cell has the cell wall, cytoplasm, nucleus and vacuole labelled.
A cell 75 μm long seen at ×400 is 30 mm long on the drawing: 75 μm × 400 = 30 000 μm = 30 mm.
A structure 4 cm long on a drawing made at ×200 has a real length of 4 cm ÷ 200 = 0.02 cm, or 200 μm.
drawing.watchOut: Draw with a sharp pencil and single clean lines, without shading or colour. Do not add details that the microscope did not resolve.
drawing.tip: A scale bar stays correct when you resize the drawing, because the bar is resized with the image.

contrast.en: Image size is measured on the drawing or micrograph; actual size is the real size of the structure. Never substitute one for the other.
contrast.ru: Размер изображения измеряют на рисунке или микрофотографии, а реальный размер — это размер самого объекта. Их нельзя подменять друг другом.

eukaryotic.name: Eukaryotic cells
eukaryotic.rule:
Eukaryotic cells have a nucleus surrounded by a membrane and other membrane-bound organelles, such as mitochondria. Eukaryotes are animals, plants, fungi and protists, and all of them are made of these cells.

The nuclear envelope separates the DNA from the cytoplasm. The DNA in the nucleus is packed into linear chromosomes. Membrane-bound organelles divide the cell into compartments, so different reactions can run at the same time. Some specialised cells lose their nucleus as they mature, for example mammalian red blood cells.
examples: An onion bulb cell has a nucleus and mitochondria but no chloroplasts, and it is still eukaryotic.
A human body cell has 46 linear chromosomes in its nucleus, arranged in 23 pairs.
eukaryotic.tip: On a diagram or electron micrograph, look for a nucleus with a double membrane (the nuclear envelope). Its presence shows that the cell is eukaryotic.

contrast.en: A eukaryotic cell is not necessarily a plant cell. Animal cells are eukaryotic too, although they have no cell wall or chloroplasts.
contrast.ru: Эукариотическая клетка — не обязательно растительная. Животные клетки тоже эукариотические, хотя у них нет клеточной стенки и хлоропластов.

prokaryotic.name: Prokaryotic cells (bacteria)
prokaryotic.rule:
Prokaryotic cells have no nucleus surrounded by a membrane. Prokaryotes are bacteria and archaea.

Usually the chromosome is a single circular DNA molecule. It lies in a region called the nucleoid, which has no membrane around it. Many bacteria also carry small circular DNA molecules called plasmids. Prokaryotic cells have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and ribosomes. Most bacteria have a cell wall made of peptidoglycan, but archaeal walls are made of different molecules.
examples: E. coli is about 2 μm long and has one circular chromosome in its nucleoid.
Lactobacillus bacteria in yoghurt turn lactose into lactic acid, which makes the milk thicken.
prokaryotic.watchOut: A plasmid is not the main chromosome. It is a small ring of DNA that carries extra genes, for example genes that help the bacterium survive antibiotics. The bacterium can usually survive without it.

contrast.en: A nucleoid is not a nucleus. It holds the DNA but has no membrane around it.
contrast.ru: Нуклеоид — не ядро. В нём лежит ДНК, но его не окружает мембрана.

comparison.name: Comparing eukaryotes and prokaryotes
comparison.rule:
Compare the two cell types by these features.

Nucleus: eukaryotes have a nucleus surrounded by a membrane. Prokaryotes have no nucleus: their DNA lies in a nucleoid.

Chromosomes: eukaryotes usually have several linear chromosomes. Prokaryotes usually have one circular chromosome.

Membrane-bound organelles: eukaryotes have them, such as mitochondria. Prokaryotes do not.

Size: eukaryotic cells are usually 10–100 μm. Prokaryotic cells are usually 0.1–5 μm.

Cell wall: plants, fungi and most bacteria have one. Animal cells do not.
examples: A yeast cell, 5–10 μm across, is eukaryotic because it has a nucleus and mitochondria.
Ribosomes occur in both cell types and are not membrane-bound.
comparison.tip: In a comparison answer, name one feature and give both cell types in one sentence, for example: 'Eukaryotes have a nucleus with a membrane; prokaryotes have a nucleoid with no membrane.'

contrast.en: Viruses are not prokaryotes. They are not made of cells and have no ribosomes or cytoplasm of their own.
contrast.ru: Вирусы — не прокариоты. Они не состоят из клеток и не имеют собственных рибосом и цитоплазмы.

nucleus.name: Nucleus
nucleus.rule: The nucleus is a membrane-bound organelle that contains most of the cell's DNA, arranged in chromosomes. Genes in the DNA determine which proteins the cell makes, so the nucleus controls the cell's activities. Nuclear pores in the nuclear envelope let copies of genes (mRNA) and other selected molecules pass into the cytoplasm.
nucleus.tip: Mature mammalian red cells lose their nucleus; skeletal muscle fibres commonly contain many nuclei.

cytoplasm.name: Cytoplasm
cytoplasm.rule: The cytoplasm is the region of the cell between the nucleus and the cell membrane. Many chemical reactions take place there. Enzymes in the cytoplasm speed up these reactions, so different reactions can run at the same time.
cytoplasm.tip: Glycolysis, the first stage of respiration, takes place in the cytosol, not inside mitochondria.

contrast.en: Cytosol is the watery part of the cytoplasm; the cytoplasm also contains the organelles outside the nucleus.
contrast.ru: Цитозоль — водная часть цитоплазмы; цитоплазма, помимо цитозоля, включает органоиды вне ядра.

membrane.name: Cell membrane
membrane.rule: The cell membrane is a phospholipid bilayer with proteins embedded in it. It separates the cell from its surroundings and controls which substances enter and leave. The middle of the bilayer is non-polar, so charged and polar particles cannot pass through it easily.
examples: O₂ and CO₂ pass freely (small, non-polar).
Glucose needs a transporter protein.
Ions (Na⁺, K⁺) need protein channels.

mitochondria.name: Mitochondria
mitochondria.rule: Mitochondria are organelles where most stages of aerobic respiration take place in eukaryotic cells. The overall equation is glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water. Energy released when glucose is oxidised is used on their inner membrane to make ATP. ATP then supplies energy for movement, growth and other processes.
mitochondria.tip: A muscle cell uses a lot of energy when it contracts, so it contains many mitochondria.

contrast.en: Mitochondria release energy from glucose in aerobic respiration; chloroplasts use light energy to build glucose from carbon dioxide and water.
contrast.ru: Митохондрии высвобождают энергию из глюкозы при аэробном дыхании; хлоропласты используют энергию света, чтобы синтезировать глюкозу из углекислого газа и воды.

ribosome.name: Ribosomes
ribosome.rule: Ribosomes are small structures made of ribosomal RNA (rRNA) and protein. They read the sequence of an mRNA molecule and join amino acids in the same order to make a protein. Ribosomes have no membrane and occur in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.
ribosome.tip: A pancreas cell that makes large amounts of digestive enzymes contains many ribosomes.

contrast.en: The nucleus stores DNA and copies it into mRNA; ribosomes read the mRNA and build the protein.
contrast.ru: Ядро хранит ДНК и переписывает её в мРНК; рибосома читает мРНК и собирает белок.

wall.name: Cell wall
wall.rule: A cell wall is a rigid layer outside the cell membrane. Its material depends on the organism: cellulose in plants, chitin in fungi and peptidoglycan in most bacteria. The wall resists swelling, so the cell does not burst when water enters by osmosis.
wall.watchOut: The cell wall does not control what enters the cell; the cell membrane is the selective barrier.

chloroplast.name: Chloroplast
chloroplast.rule: A chloroplast is an organelle in plant and algal cells where photosynthesis takes place. Chlorophyll in the thylakoid membranes (stacked membrane sacs) absorbs light energy. This energy drives the reactions in the stroma, the fluid inside the chloroplast, that build glucose from carbon dioxide and water.
chloroplast.tip: Chloroplasts are found mainly in green parts such as leaves. Root cells usually have none, because they get no light.

contrast.en: Chlorophyll is the green pigment that absorbs light; the chloroplast is the organelle that contains it.
contrast.ru: Хлорофилл — зелёный пигмент, который поглощает свет; хлоропласт — органоид, в котором он находится.

vacuole.name: Central vacuole in a plant cell
vacuole.rule: A plant cell's large central vacuole is a membrane-bound compartment containing cell sap. It stores substances and helps maintain turgor: water entry makes the cell contents press against the wall. Vacuoles also occur in other eukaryotes.
vacuole.tip: Loss of water can reduce turgor and cause wilting; a cell wall can remain intact even when its contents shrink.

contrast.en: Cell sap is the liquid inside the vacuole; the cytosol lies outside the vacuole, in the cytoplasm.
contrast.ru: Клеточный сок — жидкость внутри вакуоли; цитозоль лежит вне вакуоли, в цитоплазме.

animalVsPlant.shared: Typical plant and animal cells share a membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria and ribosomes; specialised cells may differ.
animalVsPlant.plantOnly: Typical plant cells have a cellulose cell wall and one large central vacuole. Photosynthetic plant cells also contain chloroplasts.

redBlood.name: Red blood cell (erythrocyte)
redBlood.rule: A red blood cell carries oxygen from the lungs to the body's tissues. Haemoglobin inside it binds oxygen where the oxygen level is high, in the lungs, and releases it where the level is low, in respiring tissues. The cell's shape and contents are adapted to this job.
examples: BICONCAVE shape: thin, with a large surface area relative to volume, so O₂ diffuses in and out quickly.
NO NUCLEUS: more room for haemoglobin (~270 million per cell).
FLEXIBLE: can squeeze through narrow capillaries.
redBlood.tip: Lifespan is about 120 days. Old cells are broken down in the spleen and liver, and their parts are recycled.

contrast.en: Red blood cells carry oxygen; white blood cells (leucocytes) defend the body against pathogens such as bacteria and viruses.
contrast.ru: Эритроциты переносят кислород, а лейкоциты защищают организм от возбудителей болезней, таких как бактерии и вирусы.

neurone.name: Neurone (nerve cell)
neurone.rule: A neurone is a nerve cell that carries electrical impulses. An impulse travels along the cell's membrane; at a synapse, the signal usually passes to the next cell by a chemical messenger. Neurones link sense organs with the central nervous system and with muscles or glands.
examples: LONG AXON: can be over 1 metre (from spinal cord to foot).
DENDRITES: branched ends receive signals from many other neurones.
MYELIN SHEATH: insulates the axon → impulses travel up to 100 m/s.
neurone.tip: Three types: sensory neurones carry impulses in from receptors to the CNS, motor neurones carry them from the CNS to muscles or glands, and relay neurones work inside the CNS.

contrast.en: A nerve is a bundle of axons from many neurones, held together by connective tissue. A single neurone is one cell.
contrast.ru: Нерв — пучок аксонов многих нейронов, скреплённых соединительной тканью. Один нейрон — это одна клетка.

sperm.name: Sperm cell (male gamete)
sperm.rule: A sperm cell is a male gamete, a sex cell that fuses with an egg cell at fertilisation. Its structure is adapted to reach the egg and enter it.
examples: TAIL (flagellum): beats like a whip to push the cell through fluid.
MANY MITOCHONDRIA in the mid-piece: aerobic respiration releases energy as ATP to power the tail.
ACROSOME at the head: releases enzymes that digest a path through the egg's outer layers.
HAPLOID nucleus: 23 chromosomes, half the 46 found in body cells.
sperm.tip: Millions are released at a time, but only one usually fertilises the egg.

contrast.en: A sperm cell is tiny and swims, whereas an egg cell does not swim by itself.
contrast.ru: Сперматозоид мелкий и плывёт сам, а яйцеклетка сама не плавает.

egg.name: Egg cell (ovum, female gamete)
egg.rule: An egg cell (ovum) is the female gamete. It is one of the largest human cells. Its cytoplasm holds stored nutrients for early development after fertilisation; in humans this store is small, and the embryo later gets its food from the mother.
examples: 23 + 23 = 46: the egg's 23 chromosomes join the sperm's 23 at fertilisation.
ZONA PELLUCIDA: a glycoprotein layer around a mammalian egg that the sperm must pass through.
egg.tip: One egg cell is released from the ovary about once a month at ovulation and survives about 24 hours in the fallopian tube (oviduct).

contrast.en: A zygote is not an egg cell. It forms when an egg and a sperm fuse, and it is the first cell of the new organism.
contrast.ru: Зигота — не яйцеклетка. Она образуется при слиянии яйцеклетки и сперматозоида и становится первой клеткой нового организма.

root.name: Root hair cell (plant)
root.rule: A root hair cell is a cell on the root's outer surface, with a long projection that grows into the soil. Water enters by osmosis, because the cell's contents have a lower water potential than the soil water. Mineral ions usually enter by active transport, moving from a lower to a higher concentration and using energy from respiration.
examples: The projection increases surface area in contact with soil water.
A typical root hair cell grows underground, where there is no light for photosynthesis, so it has no chloroplasts.
root.tip: Found in the 'zone of root hairs' just behind the growing root tip.

palisade.name: Palisade mesophyll cell (plant)
palisade.rule: A palisade mesophyll cell is a photosynthetic cell in the mesophyll, the inner tissue of a leaf. Most of the leaf's photosynthesis takes place in this layer.
examples: PACKED with CHLOROPLASTS: more chloroplasts means more light absorbed for photosynthesis.
COLUMN shape: packed tightly side by side, so the layer catches as much of the sunlight as possible.
Located JUST BELOW the upper leaf surface: closest to incoming sunlight.
palisade.tip: Below the palisade layer lies the SPONGY MESOPHYLL: its cells are loosely packed, with air spaces for gas exchange.

contrast.en: The upper epidermis is a transparent protective layer with few chloroplasts. It lets light through to the palisade layer below.
contrast.ru: Верхняя кожица — прозрачный защитный слой с небольшим числом хлоропластов. Она пропускает свет к столбчатому слою под ней.

transport.title: Movement across membranes
transport.diffusion: Diffusion — the spreading of particles from a higher to a lower concentration. It is passive: no energy is used.
transport.osmosis: Osmosis — diffusion of water across a partially permeable membrane.
transport.activeTransport: Active transport — moving a substance from lower to higher concentration. It is powered by ATP from respiration.

diffusion.name: Diffusion
diffusion.rule: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a higher to a lower concentration, caused by their random motion. Particles move in both directions, but more particles leave the more concentrated region. At equilibrium particles keep moving, but there is no net movement.
examples: O₂ moves from alveoli (high) into blood (low) by diffusion.
CO₂ moves from blood into alveoli (high → low) by diffusion.
Perfume spreads through a room by diffusion, but air currents also carry it, so the spreading is not diffusion alone.
Carbon dioxide enters a leaf through the stomata by diffusion, because photosynthesis uses it up inside the leaf.
diffusion.tip: Surface area to volume ratio (SA:V) falls as a cell or organism gets bigger. Volume grows faster than surface area, so large organisms need exchange surfaces such as villi and alveoli.

contrast.en: Diffusion moves any particles, such as gases or dissolved sugar, from high to low concentration, with or without a membrane.
contrast.ru: Диффузия переносит любые частицы, например газы или растворённый сахар, из области высокой концентрации в низкую, с мембраной или без неё.

osmosis.name: Osmosis
osmosis.rule: Osmosis is the net movement of water molecules across a partially permeable membrane, from a dilute solution to a concentrated solution. The dilute solution has a higher water potential, so water moves from higher to lower water potential.
examples: A red blood cell in a hypotonic (dilute) solution takes in water by osmosis and bursts.
A plant cell in pure water takes in water and becomes turgid (firm). Its cell wall stops it from bursting.
osmosis.tip: Say 'water potential', not just 'concentration': the dilute solution has a higher water potential, so water moves from it into the concentrated solution.

contrast.en: Osmosis moves only water across a partially permeable membrane. Dissolved solutes, such as sugar, cannot cross it.
contrast.ru: Осмос переносит только воду через полупроницаемую мембрану. Растворённые вещества (solutes), например сахар, через неё пройти не могут.

activeTransport.name: Active transport
activeTransport.rule: Active transport moves a substance across a membrane against the concentration difference, from low to high concentration. The cell uses ATP from respiration for this, and carrier proteins in the membrane move the substance.
examples: Root hair cells take up mineral ions from the soil, even when the ions are more concentrated inside the cell.
Glucose is absorbed from the small intestine into the blood, even when the blood already has a higher glucose concentration.
activeTransport.watchOut: Without oxygen, cells make less ATP, so active transport slows down or stops. Diffusion needs no ATP, so it carries on.

contrast.en: Active transport works against diffusion, using ATP to move substances into a region of higher concentration.
contrast.ru: Активный транспорт идёт против диффузии: он тратит АТФ и переносит вещества в область более высокой концентрации.

significance.name: Significance of diffusion in biology
significance.rule: Diffusion is efficient only over short distances, so exchange surfaces must be thin. Large organisms need ventilation and circulation to bring substances to every cell.
examples: The wall of an alveolus is only one cell thick, so oxygen diffuses quickly from the air into the blood.
Insect tracheae carry air close to tissues; many insects also ventilate their tracheal systems.
significance.tip: A good gas exchange surface has a large surface area, thin walls, a steep concentration difference, a moist surface and good ventilation or circulation. Name these features in any gas-exchange answer.

contrast.en: Single-celled organisms exchange gases by diffusion through the cell surface. Large multicellular organisms need specialised exchange surfaces, such as lungs, gills or leaves.
contrast.ru: Одноклеточные организмы обмениваются газами диффузией через поверхность клетки. Крупным многоклеточным организмам нужны специализированные поверхности обмена, например лёгкие, жабры или листья.

osmosisPractical.name: Practical: osmosis
osmosisPractical.rule:
Identical potato cylinders are put into sucrose solutions of different concentrations, each for the same time (for example 30 minutes). The sucrose concentration is the independent variable. The change in mass (or length) of each cylinder is the dependent variable.

In dilute solutions water enters the cells by osmosis, so the cylinder gains mass. In concentrated solutions water leaves the cells, so the cylinder loses mass.
examples: In pure water the mass of a cylinder rises from 4.00 g to 4.40 g: % change = (4.40 g − 4.00 g) ÷ 4.00 g × 100 = +10 %. In 1.0 mol/dm³ sucrose the mass falls from 4.00 g to 3.60 g: % change = (3.60 g − 4.00 g) ÷ 4.00 g × 100 = −10 %.

At 0.2 mol/dm³ the change is +4 %, and at 0.4 mol/dm³ it is −4 %. The mass does not change at about 0.3 mol/dm³ (the exact value varies between potatoes). So the water potential of the potato cells is about the same as a 0.3 mol/dm³ sucrose solution.
osmosisPractical.tip: Blot each cylinder dry with a paper towel before you weigh it. Water left on the surface adds mass and hides the real change. Keep the time, the volume of solution and the temperature the same for all cylinders.

contrast.en: Water potential is the tendency of water molecules to move out of a solution or cell. Pure water has the highest water potential; dissolved solutes lower it.
contrast.ru: Водный потенциал — это склонность молекул воды выходить из раствора или клетки. Чистая вода имеет наибольший водный потенциал; растворённые вещества его снижают.

bodySystems.title: Body Systems
bodySystems.intro: How systems coordinate: circulation, respiration, digestion, nervous, hormonal.

circulatory.title: Circulatory system
circulatory.body: The human circulatory system moves blood through the heart and blood vessels. Pulmonary circulation connects the heart and lungs; systemic circulation connects the heart and the rest of the body. Arteries lead away from the heart, veins lead towards it, and capillaries allow exchange with tissues.

heart.name: The heart — pump for life
heart.rule: The heart is a muscular pump with two atria that receive blood and two ventricles that eject it. The right side pumps to the lungs and the left side to the body. Pressure differences open and close valves, maintaining mainly one-way flow.
examples: RA receives deoxygenated blood from vena cava → RV → pulmonary artery → lungs.
LA receives oxygenated blood from pulmonary veins → LV → aorta → body.
Left ventricle wall is THICKEST — pumps blood around the entire body, needs more force.
Heart attack = blood supply to heart muscle blocked (coronary artery).
heart.tip: Remember: 'right has less might' — the right ventricle only pumps to the nearby lungs, so its wall is thinner.

contrast.en: Arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins towards it; these names do not specify oxygen content.
contrast.ru: Артерии несут кровь от сердца, вены — к нему; названия не определяются содержанием кислорода.

vessels.name: Blood vessels — arteries, veins, capillaries

examples: Pulmonary arteries lead from the right ventricle to the lungs.
Many limb veins use valves and surrounding muscle activity to assist return.

blood.name: Blood components

B lymphocytes can form antibody-secreting plasma cells; other white cells have different roles.
Platelets and clotting proteins help form a fibrin mesh.

respiratory.title: Respiratory system
respiratory.body: The respiratory system ventilates the lungs and provides a surface for gas exchange. Air passes through the trachea, bronchi and bronchioles to alveoli. Oxygen diffuses into blood and carbon dioxide diffuses out; these exchanges are distinct from cellular respiration.

pathway.name: Air pathway
pathway.rule: Conducting airways move air towards the gas-exchange surfaces: nose or mouth → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli. Mucus and cilia in parts of the airways help trap and remove particles.
examples: Trachea is ~10-12 cm long. C-shaped cartilage rings allow food to pass behind in oesophagus.
Cilia (tiny hairs) + mucus trap dust & bacteria → swept up to throat → swallowed.
Smoking destroys cilia → 'smoker's cough' as gunk can't be cleared.
Bronchitis = inflamed bronchi. Asthma = bronchioles constrict.
pathway.tip: Remember the SIZE order: trachea > bronchus > bronchiole > alveolus. Like a tree branching downward.

contrast.en: Ventilation moves air; gas exchange transfers gases across a surface; cellular respiration comprises chemical reactions.
contrast.ru: Вентиляция перемещает воздух; газообмен переносит газы через поверхность; клеточное дыхание включает химические реакции.

alveoli.name: Alveoli — gas exchange surfaces
alveoli.rule: Alveoli are small lung air sacs surrounded by capillaries. Their large total surface area and thin air–blood barrier allow rapid diffusion. Ventilation and blood flow maintain oxygen and carbon dioxide gradients; gases dissolve in the moist surface lining.
examples: Oxygen diffuses from alveolar air to blood; CO₂ diffuses in the opposite direction.
Loss of alveolar walls reduces gas-exchange surface area.

breathing.name: Breathing mechanism
breathing.rule: Ventilation moves air because pressure in the lungs differs from atmospheric pressure. During quiet inhalation, diaphragm and external intercostal contraction expands the chest and lowers lung pressure. Quiet exhalation is mainly passive recoil; forceful exhalation also uses muscles.
examples: Diaphragm is a dome-shaped sheet of muscle below lungs.
Intercostal muscles between ribs help expand chest.
Hiccup = involuntary diaphragm spasm.
Resting breath rate: 12-20/min. Exercise: up to 60+.
breathing.tip: Pressure-volume law: bigger space = lower pressure = air rushes in. This is BOYLE'S LAW applied to your chest.

digestive.title: Digestive system
digestive.body: The digestive system breaks food down mechanically and chemically, absorbs useful substances and eliminates undigested material. Most nutrient absorption occurs in the small intestine. Egestion of undigested food through the anus differs from excretion of metabolic wastes.

pathway.name: Digestive tract — the journey
pathway.rule: The alimentary canal runs from mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → rectum → anus. Waves of muscle contraction, called peristalsis, propel its contents. The liver and pancreas add secretions but food does not pass through those organs.
examples: Stomach acid provides conditions for pepsin; acid is not itself a digestive enzyme.
Most nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine; the large intestine also absorbs water and ions.
pathway.tip: Digestion breaks material down; absorption transfers substances across an epithelium.

enzymes.name: Digestive enzymes
enzymes.rule: Digestive enzymes are biological catalysts that accelerate hydrolysis of large food molecules into smaller absorbable products. Their active sites recognise particular substrates or bonds. Activity depends on temperature and pH; the optimum differs among enzymes.
examples: Amylase hydrolyses starch into smaller sugars; pepsin hydrolyses proteins into peptides.
Lipase breaks down triglycerides; bile emulsifies fat but is not an enzyme.
enzymes.watchOut: Low temperature slows enzyme activity; it does not normally denature the enzyme. Excessive heat or an unsuitable pH can change the active site and denature it.

absorption.name: Absorption in the small intestine
absorption.rule: Absorption is transfer of digested nutrients across the intestinal epithelium into blood or lymph. Villi increase the intestine's surface; microvilli are projections of the epithelial cells. Capillaries receive many soluble nutrients, while lacteals receive much of the absorbed fat in packaged form.

Fats → into LACTEALS → lymph system → eventually joins blood near heart.
Iron absorbed in upper small intestine. Vitamin B12 needs intrinsic factor from stomach.
Coeliac disease damages villi → poor absorption → malnutrition despite eating.
absorption.tip: Why huge surface area? Diffusion is faster across larger area. Villi + microvilli + 7m length = massive absorption capacity.

nervous.title: Nervous system
nervous.body: The nervous system detects stimuli, processes information and coordinates responses using neurones and supporting cells. The central nervous system comprises the brain and spinal cord; the peripheral nervous system links it with receptors, muscles, glands and other tissues.

structure.name: CNS vs PNS
structure.rule: The CNS consists of the brain and spinal cord. The PNS includes nerves and ganglia outside the CNS. Sensory pathways carry information towards the CNS; motor pathways carry commands to effectors. Somatic and autonomic motor pathways control different targets.
examples: Sensory pathways convey information towards the CNS; motor pathways lead to effectors.
Autonomic pathways regulate targets such as the heart and digestive tract.
structure.tip: Mnemonic: PNS Peripheral = body Parts. CNS Central = brain + Cord.

neurone.name: Neurone structure
neurone.rule: A typical neurone has a cell body, dendrites that receive input and an axon that conducts action potentials. Myelin insulates some axons and speeds conduction between gaps in the sheath. Most synapses transmit to the next cell using neurotransmitters.
examples: Longest neurone in human body: from base of spinal cord to big toe (~1 m).
White matter contains many myelinated axons; grey matter contains many neuronal cell bodies, dendrites and synapses.
Multiple sclerosis = autoimmune attack on myelin → signals slow/fail.
Speed: myelinated axons conduct at up to 120 m/s. Unmyelinated: ~1 m/s.
neurone.tip: Myelin enables rapid conduction between nodes of Ranvier; the wire-insulation analogy does not explain all neuronal signalling.

reflex.name: Reflex arc — fast involuntary response
reflex.rule: A reflex arc is the pathway producing an automatic response to a stimulus: receptor → sensory neurone → CNS connection → motor neurone → effector. Some arcs include relay neurones; others do not. Reflexes may be integrated in the spinal cord or brainstem.
examples: The knee-jerk reflex has a direct sensory-to-motor synapse in its main pathway.
A withdrawal reflex uses interneurones and can begin without a conscious decision.
reflex.watchOut: Some reflexes are integrated in the brainstem; a reflex is not defined by complete absence of brain involvement.

nutrition.title: Nutrition & balanced diet
nutrition.body: Nutrition supplies matter and energy needed for maintenance, growth and activity. A balanced diet provides adequate energy, essential nutrients, fibre and water in suitable proportions. Requirements vary with development, body size, activity and health.

groups.name: The 7 food groups
groups.rule: Carbohydrates and fats supply energy; fats also form membranes. Proteins supply amino acids for body proteins. Vitamins and minerals support specific functions, fibre supports intestinal function, and water acts as a solvent and transport medium. These are nutrient categories, not seven mutually exclusive foods.
examples: Vitamin C deficiency can cause scurvy; iron deficiency can contribute to anaemia.
Different foods supply overlapping combinations of nutrients.
groups.tip: Nutrient adequacy matters; omitting one named food does not automatically cause deficiency if nutrients come from other sources.

energy.name: Energy requirements
energy.rule: Energy requirements are the dietary energy needed to support metabolism, physical activity and growth. They are commonly expressed in kJ or kcal, with 1 kcal = 4.184 kJ. Basal metabolic rate is energy use measured at rest under specified conditions.
examples: Two people of the same age may have different needs because body size and activity differ.
A food-energy comparison should use the same units and portion size.
energy.tip: Approximate metabolizable energy: carbohydrate and protein 17 kJ/g; fat 37 kJ/g. Values depend on composition.

deficiency.name: Malnutrition — overnutrition and undernutrition
deficiency.rule: Malnutrition is a deficiency, excess or imbalance in energy or nutrient intake. It includes undernutrition, micronutrient deficiencies and overweight or obesity. A person can consume excess energy while lacking particular nutrients; malnutrition is not synonymous with starvation.
examples: A person may have sufficient total energy intake but an iron deficiency.
Growth, nutrient status and clinical context matter when assessing malnutrition.

respiration.title: Respiration — aerobic, anaerobic, exercise
respiration.body: Cellular respiration is a set of metabolic reactions that transfers energy from fuels such as glucose into forms cells can use, including ATP. Aerobic respiration uses oxygen; some microorganisms respire without it. Fermentation is another anaerobic pathway, often grouped with anaerobic respiration in school courses.

aerobic.name: Aerobic respiration
aerobic.rule: Aerobic respiration oxidises fuels using oxygen as the final electron acceptor. The overall glucose equation is C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O. Some released energy supports ATP synthesis and some becomes heat; ATP yield is not a fixed coefficient in this equation.
examples: In eukaryotes, glycolysis occurs in cytosol and later aerobic stages occur in mitochondria.
Plants carry out cellular respiration in light and darkness.
aerobic.tip: ATP is a molecule used in energy transfer, not a synonym for energy itself.

contrast.en: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen. Fermentation does not use an electron-transport chain; strict anaerobic respiration uses another final electron acceptor.

anaerobic.name: Anaerobic respiration
anaerobic.rule: Fermentation lets glycolysis continue without oxygen by regenerating NAD⁺. Glycolysis yields a net 2 ATP per glucose. Animal cells can form lactate; yeast can form ethanol and CO₂. exercise.name: Body's response to exercise
exercise.rule: During exercise, active muscles need faster ATP production. Increased heart output, ventilation and blood flow to muscles support oxygen delivery and carbon dioxide removal. Both aerobic metabolism and anaerobic ATP-producing pathways contribute; their relative contributions depend on intensity and duration.
examples: Heart output and ventilation usually rise as muscle activity increases.
The energy contribution of each pathway changes with exercise intensity and duration.
exercise.tip: After exercise, oxygen consumption supports recovery, including restoration of energy stores and use of lactate; it is not simply a debt repaid by destroying lactic acid.

endocrine.title: Endocrine (hormonal) system
endocrine.body: The endocrine system coordinates activity through hormones released into the blood. Only cells with suitable receptors respond to a particular hormone. Hormones regulate processes such as metabolism, growth, reproduction and blood glucose; their speed and duration vary.

comparison.name: Endocrine vs Nervous — different speeds
comparison.rule: Nervous signalling uses electrical activity along neurones and signals at synapses; endocrine signalling carries hormones in blood. Nervous responses are often rapid and targeted, whereas hormonal effects often develop more slowly and last longer. These are tendencies, not absolute rules.
examples: Reflex (nervous): pain → response in 50 ms.
Adrenaline (endocrine): scary event → rush throughout body in seconds, lasts minutes.
Insulin (endocrine): blood sugar regulation lasts hours.
Growth hormone (endocrine): operates over months and years.
comparison.tip: Often work TOGETHER. Stress: brain (nervous) signals adrenal glands (endocrine) → adrenaline releases → effects everywhere.

hormones.name: Key hormones
hormones.rule: A hormone is a chemical messenger released by endocrine cells that changes the activity of receptor-bearing target cells. Insulin promotes processes that lower blood glucose; glucagon promotes processes that raise it. Feedback helps maintain glucose within a regulated range.
examples: INSULIN (pancreas, β cells): lowers blood sugar — promotes glucose uptake into cells, conversion to glycogen.
GLUCAGON (pancreatic α cells): raises blood glucose by stimulating liver glycogen breakdown and glucose production and release.
ADRENALINE (adrenal glands): fight-or-flight — raises heart rate, releases sugar, dilates pupils.
OESTROGEN (ovaries): female puberty, menstrual cycle. TESTOSTERONE (testes): male puberty, sex drive.
THYROXINE (thyroid): metabolic rate. INSULIN and THYROXINE are exam favourites.
hormones.tip: Negative feedback regulates most hormones. Blood sugar too high → insulin out → lowers it → less insulin needed. Self-correcting.

diabetes.name: Diabetes — when blood sugar control fails
diabetes.rule: Diabetes mellitus involves persistently elevated blood glucose. In type 1, destruction of pancreatic beta cells causes severe insulin deficiency. In type 2, reduced insulin responsiveness and insufficient insulin secretion both contribute. Either type can occur at different ages.
examples: Type 1 involves severe insulin deficiency; type 2 includes insulin resistance and impaired secretion.

photosynthesis.title: Photosynthesis & Biotechnology
photosynthesis.intro: How plants make food from light, and how humans use biology to engineer organisms. The exam will assess the process of photosynthesis and the applications of genetic engineering.

equation.name: The word and balanced equation
equation.rule: Photosynthesis uses light energy to build organic molecules from carbon dioxide. In plants, water supplies electrons and oxygen is released. The simplified net equation is 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂, with light and chlorophyll required; light is an energy input, not matter.
examples: Carbon dioxide + water → carbohydrate + oxygen, using light energy.
Plants respire in daylight too; net gas exchange depends on both rates.
equation.tip: Memorise the equation in BOTH word and balanced form. Note: water and CO₂ are the inputs — light is energy, not a reactant.

contrast.en: Carbon dioxide and water supply matter; light supplies energy. Plants also respire in both light and darkness.
contrast.ru: Углекислый газ и вода поставляют вещество, свет — энергию. Растения дышат и на свету, и в темноте.

location.name: Where photosynthesis happens
location.rule: In plants and algae, photosynthesis occurs in chloroplasts. Chlorophyll and other pigments in thylakoid membranes absorb light. Carbon fixation occurs in the stroma. Leaf mesophyll contains many chloroplasts, but photosynthetic bacteria have no chloroplasts.
examples: Thylakoid membranes contain light-absorbing pigment systems.
Xylem supplies water; phloem transports organic solutes, commonly sucrose.

factors.name: Limiting factors
factors.rule: A limiting factor is a condition whose change would increase the photosynthesis rate while other conditions remain fixed. Light intensity, CO₂ availability and temperature can each limit rate. Raising one factor may eventually stop helping because another becomes limiting; excessive heat can reduce enzyme activity.
examples: Increasing light at fixed CO₂ and temperature can produce an initial rise followed by a plateau.
Water shortage can close stomata and limit CO₂ entry.
factors.watchOut: An optimum temperature depends on the species and conditions; a single universal value is inappropriate.

uses.name: What plants do with glucose
uses.rule: Photosynthetic carbohydrates supply carbon and energy for growth. Plants use them in respiration, store carbon as starch, build cellulose and make other organic molecules. Protein synthesis also requires mineral nutrients such as nitrogen; glucose alone cannot supply nitrogen atoms.
examples: Potatoes/grain — starch stores.
Cellulose in walls makes wood, cotton, paper.
Plant proteins (e.g., soya) made from amino acids derived from glucose + N.
Glucose can also be converted to fats (in seeds — high-energy storage for the embryo).
uses.tip: The Calvin cycle first produces three-carbon compounds; glucose is a convenient product in the simplified overall equation.

experiments.name: Classic photosynthesis experiments
experiments.rule: Photosynthesis experiments test a stated prediction using a control and measured outcomes. A leaf starch test gives indirect evidence of carbohydrate accumulation; oxygen production can estimate net photosynthetic rate. Respiration and storage can affect results, so neither measure directly counts every photosynthetic reaction.
examples: Compare covered and uncovered parts of a previously destarched leaf using an appropriate control.
Measure gas volume rather than assuming all pondweed bubbles have equal volume.
experiments.tip: All these test ONE variable while controlling others — exactly what Criterion B is about.

definition.name: What is genetic engineering?
definition.rule: Genetic engineering is deliberate modification of genetic material using molecular techniques. It can insert, remove or alter DNA sequences, including changes within a species. Transferring a gene between species is one example; selective breeding chooses parents without directly editing their DNA.
examples: Engineered microbes can produce a human insulin protein.
Editing a plant gene without adding another species' DNA is also genetic engineering.
definition.tip: Targeted editing can affect more than the intended trait; verify the sequence and phenotype.

contrast.en: Biotechnology is broader than genetic engineering; engineering can edit existing DNA without adding a gene from another species.
contrast.ru: Биотехнология шире генной инженерии; инженерное изменение ДНК не обязательно переносит ген другого вида.

techniques.name: Key techniques
techniques.rule: Recombinant-DNA methods join DNA sequences, often using restriction enzymes, ligase and a vector such as a plasmid. Gene-editing systems such as CRISPR direct changes to selected sites. Successful delivery does not guarantee correct expression; the modified cells must be checked.
examples: Restriction enzymes cut selected DNA sequences; ligase joins DNA backbones.
A guide RNA can direct a CRISPR-associated enzyme to a selected DNA region.
techniques.watchOut: Precision is a goal, not a guarantee: off-target and unintended on-target changes must be assessed.

applications.name: Applications — medicine, agriculture, industry
applications.rule: Applications of genetic engineering include producing human insulin in microbes, modifying crop traits and investigating gene function. Some treatments alter patient cells to address disease. Each application needs separate evidence of effectiveness and effects; a useful gene does not guarantee a useful organism.
examples: Recombinant protein production uses modified cells as factories for a chosen protein.
A herbicide-tolerance trait changes a crop's response to a particular herbicide.
applications.tip: When asked about benefits/risks: split into ENVIRONMENTAL (good: less pesticide; bad: gene flow to wild plants), SOCIAL (good: cheaper food; bad: dependence on big agri companies), ECONOMIC, ETHICAL.

ethics.name: Ethical and biological concerns
ethics.rule: Ethical assessment of genetic engineering considers likely benefits, evidence about harms, animal welfare, consent where relevant and fair access. Environmental assessment considers gene flow and effects on ecosystems. Biological risk and value judgements are different questions and both require explicit reasoning.
examples: Assess gene flow to relatives using evidence about the particular organism and environment.
Discuss who receives benefits, bears risks and can participate in decisions.
ethics.watchOut: Separate evidence about biological effects from ethical judgements; explain each rather than assuming every application has the same outcome.

ecology.title: Ecology
ecology.intro: How organisms interact with each other and the environment. Energy flow, nutrient cycles, human impacts.

levels.title: Levels of organisation
levels.body: An individual is one organism. A population is individuals of one species in a defined area; a community includes populations of different species. An ecosystem includes the community, its non-living environment and their interactions. The biosphere includes Earth's ecosystems.

carbonCycle.title: Carbon cycle
carbonCycle.body: The carbon cycle is movement of carbon among organisms, air, water, soil and rocks. Photosynthesis incorporates CO₂ into organic matter; respiration, decomposition and combustion return carbon to the environment. Fossil-fuel combustion moves long-stored carbon into the active cycle.

dna.title: DNA
dna.body: DNA stores hereditary information in its nucleotide sequence. In a double helix, A pairs with T and C with G. A gene is a DNA sequence whose expression produces a functional RNA or protein. Most human body cells have 46 nuclear chromosomes; gametes have 23.

contrast.en: DNA is a molecule; a gene is a functional sequence; a chromosome contains a long DNA molecule with associated proteins.

mitosis.title: Mitosis
mitosis.body: Mitosis is nuclear division that separates duplicated chromosomes into two nuclei with the same chromosome set. It commonly accompanies cytokinesis to produce two daughter cells for growth, repair or asexual reproduction. It preserves ploidy; it does not necessarily produce diploid cells.

contrast.en: Mitosis divides the nucleus; cytokinesis divides the cell. Mitosis preserves ploidy, including in haploid cells.
contrast.ru: Митоз делит ядро, цитокинез — клетку. Митоз сохраняет плоидность, в том числе в гаплоидных клетках.

meiosis.title: Meiosis
meiosis.body: Meiosis consists of two nuclear divisions after one DNA replication, reducing the chromosome set from diploid to haploid. Homologous chromosomes separate first and sister chromatids second. It creates genetic variation and produces gametes in animals, but spores in many plants and fungi.

contrast.en: Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes; meiosis II separates sister chromatids. DNA is not replicated between the two divisions.
contrast.ru: В мейозе I расходятся гомологичные хромосомы, в мейозе II — сестринские хроматиды. Между делениями ДНК не удваивается.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.body: Inheritance is transmission of genetic information between generations. Alleles are alternative sequences at a gene locus. With complete dominance, a heterozygote shows the dominant phenotype; other relationships include incomplete dominance and codominance. A Punnett square predicts probabilities under specified assumptions.

contrast.en: Genotype is genetic constitution; phenotype is an observable characteristic influenced by genotype and environment.
contrast.ru: Генотип — генетическая конституция; фенотипический признак зависит от генотипа и среды.

variation.title: Variation
variation.body: Variation means differences among individuals. Genetic differences, environmental influences and their interaction affect traits. Continuous variation gives a range of measured values, such as height; discontinuous variation gives categories, such as ABO blood group. The graph type depends on the data and the question.

sources.name: Sources of variation
sources.rule: Mutations create new DNA sequence variants. Recombination and fertilisation combine existing variants in new ways. Environment also affects phenotype, and a genetic effect can depend on the environment. A percentage attributed to heredity is a population estimate under specified conditions, not a fixed share of one person's trait.
examples: Mutation may create a new allele; meiosis can produce new combinations of existing alleles.
Nutrition can affect height, alongside inherited differences.
sources.tip: Mutation creates new alleles; meiosis and fertilisation create new combinations. Gene flow can introduce existing alleles into another population.

continuous.name: Continuous vs discontinuous variation
continuous.rule: Continuous variation can take intermediate values within a range; discontinuous variation is recorded in distinct categories. Height is continuous and ABO blood group is categorical. A continuous distribution need not be bell-shaped, and a categorical trait need not be controlled by only one gene.
examples: Height measured in centimetres: a numerical variable with many intermediate values.
ABO group A, B, AB or O: categories without numerical spacing.
continuous.tip: Use a histogram for a numerical distribution and a scatter plot for a relationship between numerical variables.

contrast.en: Genotype is genetic constitution; phenotype is an observable characteristic influenced by genotype and environment.
contrast.ru: Генотип — генетическая конституция; фенотипический признак зависит от генотипа и среды.

evolution.title: Evolution by natural selection
evolution.body: Evolution is change in heritable characteristics of populations across generations. Natural selection is one mechanism: individuals with some inherited variants leave more surviving offspring in a given environment. Mutation, genetic drift and gene flow also change populations.

naturalSelection.name: Natural selection — 4 steps
naturalSelection.rule: Natural selection occurs when heritable differences affect reproductive success. If a variant increases the number of surviving offspring in a particular environment, it can become more common over generations. Individuals do not acquire needed mutations on purpose, and populations evolve rather than individual organisms.
examples: An antibiotic can favour bacteria carrying resistance variants, increasing their frequency.
An advantage depends on the environment and may disappear when conditions change.
naturalSelection.tip: Heritable variation → differences in reproductive success → changed variant frequencies. This describes selection, not every evolutionary mechanism.

contrast.en: Individuals develop during life; populations evolve over generations. Natural selection is one mechanism of evolution.
contrast.ru: Особи развиваются в течение жизни; популяции эволюционируют в поколениях. Естественный отбор — один из механизмов эволюции.

speciation.name: Speciation — how new species form
speciation.rule: Speciation is the formation of distinct evolutionary lineages recognised as species. Under the biological species concept, reproductive isolation restricts gene flow between populations. This concept is useful for many sexually reproducing organisms but has limits for fossils, asexual organisms and hybridising populations.
examples: Geographic separation can reduce gene flow and allow divergence.
Different breeding seasons or mating signals can contribute to reproductive isolation.
speciation.watchOut: Isolation does not guarantee eventual speciation; species boundaries can be incomplete where hybridisation occurs.

evidence.name: Evidence for evolution
evidence.rule: Evidence for evolution includes the ordered fossil record, shared anatomical patterns, similarities in DNA and observed population change. Independent observations support common ancestry and test hypotheses about relationships. Similar appearance alone can arise by convergence and does not establish close ancestry.
examples: Shared arrangements of limb bones can support homology despite different uses.
DNA comparisons test relatedness using many sequences, not one visual resemblance.
evidence.tip: Use several independent lines of evidence to evaluate an evolutionary explanation.

humanEvolution.name: Human evolution
humanEvolution.rule: Human evolution is the branching history of the lineage leading to Homo sapiens and its extinct relatives. Humans are great apes and share ancestors with other living apes. Fossil and genetic evidence indicates African origins and later migrations, with interbreeding among some human lineages.
examples: Different ancient human lineages overlapped in time; evolution is a branching tree.
Some modern populations carry inherited DNA from Neanderthal or Denisovan admixture.
humanEvolution.tip: Humans descend from ancestral apes and share ancestors with other living apes; humans did not evolve from living chimpanzees.

immune.title: Health & Disease
immune.intro: How the body stays healthy and defends itself. This page covers infectious and non-communicable diseases, pathogens, the body's defences, vaccination and antibiotics.

communicable.name: Communicable (infectious) diseases
communicable.rule:
A communicable disease is caused by a pathogen and can pass from one person to another, directly or indirectly.

The pathogen can travel through direct contact, including contact with bodily fluids, in droplets from coughs and sneezes, through contaminated food or water, or through a vector. A vector is an organism that carries a pathogen from one host to another, such as a mosquito.
examples: Tuberculosis (TB) is caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis and spreads through the air when an infected person coughs.
Influenza (flu) is caused by a virus and spreads in tiny droplets from the coughs and sneezes of infected people.
Malaria is caused by a protist (Plasmodium) and is spread by the bite of an infected Anopheles mosquito.
Athlete's foot is caused by a fungus and spreads by contact in damp places, such as showers and changing rooms.
Hepatitis B is a viral infection of the liver that spreads through infected blood and other bodily fluids, for example through shared needles or unprotected sex.
Cholera is caused by a bacterium that spreads through water or food contaminated with faeces.
communicable.tip: When you write about an infection, state the type of pathogen and the transmission route.

contrast.en: Infection means a pathogen has entered the body and is multiplying there. Disease means the infection is causing harm to the body, usually with symptoms. A person can be infected with no symptoms and still pass the pathogen on.
contrast.ru: Инфекция — это попадание патогена в организм и его размножение в нём. Болезнь — это вред, который инфекция наносит организму, обычно с симптомами. Человек может быть инфицирован без симптомов и всё же передать патоген другим людям.

nonCommunicable.name: Non-communicable diseases
nonCommunicable.rule:
A non-communicable disease cannot be passed from one person to another, and it is usually not caused by a pathogen.

Causes include genes, problems with body processes such as insulin production, the environment and behaviour. Many chronic (long-lasting) diseases belong to this group, for example heart disease and some cancers.
examples: Cystic fibrosis is inherited: a faulty gene makes the body produce thick mucus that blocks the airways in the lungs and the ducts of the pancreas.
nonCommunicable.watchOut: Some diseases have mixed causes. Cervical cancer is usually caused by a long-lasting infection with human papillomavirus (HPV), but the cancer itself is not passed from person to person.
nonCommunicable.tip: To explain a non-communicable disease, identify one specific cause and show how it affects the body.

contrast.en: A disease can be inherited and still not be communicable. Inheritance means passing genes from parents to children. Communicability means that a pathogen can pass from one person to another.
contrast.ru: Болезнь может наследоваться и при этом не быть инфекционной. Наследование — это передача генов от родителей к детям. Инфекционность — это способность патогена переходить от одного человека к другому.

lifestyle.name: Lifestyle risk factors
lifestyle.rule:
A risk factor is a behaviour or condition linked to a higher chance of developing a disease. Smoking, a diet high in salt, sugar or fat, physical inactivity and heavy drinking are lifestyle risk factors.

A risk factor works through a chain of events in the body. For example, physical inactivity and a diet high in sugar can lead to obesity. Obesity raises the risk of type 2 diabetes.
examples: Smoking raises the risk of lung cancer and heart disease. Stopping smoking lowers this risk over time.
lifestyle.tip: When you write about a habit, state that it increases the risk of a disease rather than that it causes it.

contrast.en: Risk factors can be modifiable or non-modifiable. Smoking and diet can be changed, but age and family history cannot. Both types still raise the risk of disease.
contrast.ru: Факторы риска бывают изменяемыми (modifiable) и неизменяемыми (non-modifiable). Курение и питание можно изменить, а возраст и наследственность — нельзя. Оба вида всё равно повышают риск болезни.

global.name: Global patterns of disease
global.rule: Global patterns of disease show how common illness and early death are in different parts of the world. They depend on the age structure of the population, the environment, exposure to pathogens and risk factors, sanitation and access to healthcare.
examples: In many wealthy countries, non-communicable diseases cause most deaths. In some poorer regions, infections such as diarrhoea from dirty water still cause many child deaths.
Malaria is found mainly in tropical and subtropical regions, where the warm climate suits the mosquitoes that carry the malaria parasite.
global.tip: When you write about a global pattern, state the region, the year of the data and one cause.

contrast.en: A large number of cases does not mean a high rate. The rate compares cases with the size of the population, so a large country can have many cases and still a low risk for each person.
contrast.ru: Большое число случаев ещё не значит высокую заболеваемость (rate). Заболеваемость сравнивает число случаев с размером населения, поэтому в большой стране случаев может быть много, а риск для каждого человека — низкий.

pathogens.title: Types of pathogen
pathogens.body: A pathogen is an agent, usually a microorganism, that causes disease. Pathogens fall mainly into four groups: bacteria, viruses, fungi and protists. Most microorganisms are harmless or useful, so being a microorganism does not make something a pathogen.

bacteria.name: Bacterial pathogens
bacteria.rule: Bacteria are single-celled prokaryotes: their cells have no nucleus, and their DNA lies free in the cytoplasm. Pathogenic bacteria damage tissues or release toxins. They reproduce by binary fission, splitting in two, so a small number of bacteria can quickly become a large population.
examples: Salmonella is a bacterium spread in contaminated food, such as poultry or eggs. It causes diarrhoea, fever and vomiting.
Gonorrhoea is a bacterial sexually transmitted infection. If it is not treated, it can cause infertility.
Tuberculosis (TB) is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, a slow-growing bacterium. Treatment with antibiotics takes several months.
Cholera is caused by the bacterium Vibrio cholerae. It releases a toxin that causes severe diarrhoea and dehydration.
MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) is a bacterium that is resistant to many antibiotics, so its infections are harder to treat.
bacteria.tip: In an exam, say how an antibiotic works. For example, it can damage the bacterial cell wall or block protein synthesis in bacterial ribosomes.

viruses.name: Viral pathogens
viruses.rule: A virus is a non-cellular agent: a DNA or RNA genome inside a protein coat, sometimes with an outer lipid envelope. It reproduces only inside a host cell, where the cell's machinery makes copies of the virus's genome and coat proteins. New viruses leave the cell, often destroying it.
examples: Influenza (flu): the virus mutates quickly, so the flu vaccine is updated every year.

HIV infects T-helper lymphocytes and weakens the immune system. It is transmitted through infected blood, semen, vaginal fluid and breast milk, for example during unprotected sex. Untreated, it can lead to AIDS.
Measles, mumps and rubella are viral childhood diseases. The MMR vaccine prevents them.

COVID-19 is caused by SARS-CoV-2, a coronavirus identified in early 2020 after an outbreak of pneumonia in late 2019. It spreads in droplets that an infected person releases when breathing, coughing or talking. It led to a worldwide pandemic from 2020.
Tobacco mosaic virus infects plants. Its pale, mottled patches on the leaves reduce photosynthesis.
viruses.watchOut: Asking for antibiotics for a cold or flu is a common mistake. Unnecessary courses do not help the patient and make bacteria resistant, so the drugs may stop working when they are really needed.

contrast.en: A virus is not a tiny cell. It has no cytoplasm and no ribosomes, so it cannot make proteins until it enters a host cell.
contrast.ru: Вирус — не маленькая клетка. У него нет цитоплазмы и рибосом, поэтому белки он сам не синтезирует, пока не попадёт в клетку-хозяина.

fungi.name: Fungal pathogens
fungi.rule: Fungal pathogens are eukaryotes: their cells have a nucleus. They include single-celled yeasts and filamentous fungi, whose bodies are made of hyphae (thin threads). Fungal cell walls contain chitin, which bacterial cell walls do not.
examples: Athlete's foot is a fungal infection caused by Trichophyton. It gives an itchy, scaly rash between the toes.
Ringworm causes a red, ring-shaped, itchy rash on the skin. It spreads by contact with an infected person, an animal or an object.
Thrush is an overgrowth of the yeast Candida. It can follow a course of antibiotics, which kill the bacteria that normally keep the yeast in check.
Aspergillus is a fungus that can infect the lungs of people with a weak immune system.
Powdery mildew is a fungal disease that coats rose leaves with a white, powdery layer.
fungi.tip: Fungi grow best in warm, damp conditions. If a question asks about prevention, explain that keeping the skin dry lowers the risk.

contrast.en: The English name ringworm is misleading. It is caused by a fungus, not a worm, so anti-worm medicines do not work against it.
contrast.ru: Английское название ringworm («кольцевой червь») вводит в заблуждение. Болезнь вызывает гриб, а не червь, поэтому средства от глистов не помогают.

protists.name: Protist pathogens
protists.rule: Pathogenic protists are single-celled eukaryotes: their cells have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. Many are parasites that live in or on a host and harm it.
examples: Toxoplasmosis is caused by the protist Toxoplasma gondii. It spreads through undercooked meat or contact with cat faeces.
Amoebic dysentery is caused by the protist Entamoeba histolytica. It spreads in food or water contaminated with faeces and causes bloody diarrhoea.
protists.watchOut: Antibiotics act on bacterial structures, such as the cell wall. The malaria parasite has no such wall, so malaria is usually treated with antimalarial medicines instead.

contrast.en: The pathogen and its vector are different. In malaria, Plasmodium is the pathogen and the mosquito is only the vector, so the mosquito does not cause the disease.
contrast.ru: Патоген и вектор — разные вещи. При малярии патоген — плазмодий, а комар только переносит его, поэтому комар сам болезнь не вызывает.

barriers.title: Transmission barriers and body defence
barriers.body:
Transmission barriers keep pathogens from getting inside the body. They are non-specific: they work in the same way against all pathogens.

The main barriers are:

- skin: unbroken skin is a physical barrier, but a cut is an entry point for bacteria
- mucus in the airways: sticky mucus traps dust, bacteria and viruses
- ciliated epithelium: the cells lining the airways have cilia, which beat and move the mucus up to the throat, where it is swallowed
- stomach acid: hydrochloric acid (pH around 2) kills most microbes swallowed with food
- tears: they contain lysozyme, an enzyme that breaks down the cell walls of some bacteria

Example: bacteria in the dust you breathe in stick to the mucus in your windpipe, and the mucus is then swallowed and carried to the stomach.

Body defence summary: the body defends itself in two lines. The first line, the barriers above, keeps out most pathogens.

contrast.en: Transmission barriers are the body's first line of defence. They are present from birth and work all the time. Unlike the immune system, they do not get stronger after an infection.
contrast.ru: Барьеры передачи — это первая линия защиты. Они есть с рождения и работают постоянно. В отличие от иммунной системы, после болезни они не становятся сильнее.

immuneResponse.title: Immune system (second line of defence)
immuneResponse.body:
The immune system is the second line of defence. It deals with pathogens that get past the barriers, using phagocytes, lymphocytes, antibodies and memory cells.

Phagocytes are white blood cells that engulf pathogens. A phagocyte surrounds a pathogen and takes it inside, where the cell's enzymes digest it.

This process is called phagocytosis. It works against any pathogen, so it is non-specific.

Lymphocytes are white blood cells. Each one recognises one specific antigen, and B-lymphocytes then make antibodies against it. An antibody fits its antigen like a key fits a lock.

Memory cells are lymphocytes that stay in the body after an infection. If the same pathogen returns, they respond faster and make more antibodies, so the illness is usually stopped before it becomes serious.

Example: after chickenpox, memory cells usually stop you catching it again.

contrast.en: An antibody is a protein that the body makes in response to an antigen. Do not confuse the two: the antigen is the marker on the pathogen; the antibody is the body's reaction to it.
contrast.ru: Антитело — белок, который организм вырабатывает в ответ на антиген. Не путай их: антиген — метка на поверхности патогена, а антитело — ответ организма на неё.

vaccination.title: Vaccination
vaccination.body:
Vaccination gives the immune system a safe way to meet a pathogen. A vaccine contains weakened or killed pathogens, or only parts of them, such as an antigen from the pathogen's surface. The immune system then makes antibodies and memory cells, but the person does not get the disease.

Example: the MMR vaccine contains a weakened measles virus. If the person later meets the real virus, the memory cells respond quickly, and the virus is usually destroyed before it causes illness.

contrast.en: Vaccination is the act of giving a vaccine; immunity is the state of being protected from a disease. Do not confuse them: a vaccine helps prevent illness, but it does not cure one that has already started.
contrast.ru: Вакцинация — это введение вакцины, а иммунитет — состояние защищённости от болезни. Не путай их: вакцина помогает не заболеть, но не лечит уже начавшуюся болезнь.

antibiotics.title: Antibiotics
antibiotics.body:
Antibiotics are medicines that kill bacteria or stop them from growing. Some antibiotics damage the cell wall or stop bacteria building it, so the cell bursts. Others block protein synthesis in bacterial ribosomes, so the bacterium cannot make the proteins it needs.

Human cells have no cell wall, and their ribosomes are different, so antibiotics mainly harm bacteria. For example, penicillin stops bacteria building their cell walls, so it can treat a bacterial infection such as strep throat.

A bacterial population can become resistant to an antibiotic. Some bacteria are already resistant before the drug is used, because of random mutations or gene transfer. The antibiotic does not cause this change: it kills susceptible bacteria, and the resistant survivors reproduce and pass the ability to survive the drug on to their offspring.

Frequent use, or a course that is not finished, lets more resistant bacteria survive. The trait belongs to the bacteria, not to the patient's body.

Antibiotics do not act on viruses, so they are not used for viral infections, and a doctor decides which drug to take and how long the course lasts.

A new antibiotic goes through drug development before a doctor can prescribe it. First comes pre-clinical testing in the laboratory, on cells and animals.

Clinical trials then test the drug on people in phases. Phase 1 checks safety in a small group, Phase 2 checks effectiveness and side effects in patients, and Phase 3 compares the drug with existing treatments in a large group.

contrast.en: An antibiotic is not a vaccine: it treats a bacterial infection that has already started, and it does not create immunity.
contrast.ru: Антибиотик — не вакцина: он лечит уже начавшуюся бактериальную инфекцию и не создаёт иммунитет.

immuneSystem.def: The immune system is the network of cells, molecules, tissues and organs that detects and responds to infection and other threats. It includes innate and adaptive defences; immune responses can sometimes also damage the body's own tissues.

contrast.en: Innate defence acts broadly; adaptive immunity recognises particular antigens and can form memory.

cellularRespiration.def: Cellular respiration transfers energy from nutrient oxidation into ATP. Aerobic respiration uses oxygen; anaerobic respiration in some microorganisms uses other final electron acceptors. Fermentation is a distinct pathway often grouped with anaerobic respiration at school level.

contrast.en: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen. Fermentation does not use an electron-transport chain; strict anaerobic respiration uses another final electron acceptor.
contrast.ru: Аэробное дыхание использует кислород. При брожении нет дыхательной цепи; при анаэробном дыхании в строгом смысле конечный акцептор электронов иной.

photosynthesis.def: Photosynthesis is the use of light energy to build organic substances from CO₂. Plants, algae and cyanobacteria use water and release O₂. Some other photosynthetic bacteria use different electron donors and do not release oxygen.

ecosystem.def: An ecosystem is a community of organisms interacting with one another and with the non-living environment in a defined area. Its boundary is chosen for the study; it need not be a closed system.

dna.def: DNA, deoxyribonucleic acid, is the polymer whose nucleotide sequence stores hereditary information in cells. DNA is organised into chromosomes; a gene is a functional region of DNA, not a whole chromosome.

contrast.en: DNA is a molecule; a gene is a functional sequence; a chromosome contains a long DNA molecule with associated proteins.

evolution.def: Evolution is change in inherited characteristics of populations over generations. Natural selection, mutation, genetic drift and gene flow can contribute. Evolution is not necessarily progress towards greater complexity.

contrast.ru: Особи развиваются в течение жизни; популяции эволюционируют в поколениях. Естественный отбор — один из механизмов эволюции.

mitosis.def: Mitosis is nuclear division that distributes duplicated chromosomes into two nuclei while preserving chromosome number. It usually accompanies cell division; mutation aside, the resulting nuclei contain matching genetic information.

contrast.en: Mitosis divides the nucleus; cytokinesis divides the cell. Mitosis preserves ploidy, including in haploid cells.

meiosis.def: Meiosis is two successive nuclear divisions following one DNA replication, usually producing four haploid nuclear products from one diploid cell. Recombination and chromosome segregation generate different allele combinations.

contrast.en: Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes; meiosis II separates sister chromatids. DNA is not replicated between the two divisions.
